config.title: Discriminated Union Props

intro.title: Discriminated Union Props
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays different types of notifications, such as success, warning, and error messages. You will learn how to use discriminated union props in TypeScript to define a prop that can be one of several specific shapes, each identified by a common 'type' property. This involves creating a union type for the props and using type narrowing to safely access the correct data for each notification variant. By the end, you'll understand how to make your components more type-safe and expressive when handling multiple related data structures.
intro.usecase: Discriminated union props are essential when building UI components that need to handle multiple distinct states or variants. You'll use this pattern in dashboard components that switch between loading, error, and data display states, or in form controls that toggle between different input types like text, select, or date picker. This approach ensures type safety when implementing modals with different actions, navigation menus with varied item types, or data visualization panels that render charts, tables, or empty states. By using discriminated unions, you create robust components that prevent invalid state combinations while providing clear developer experience through TypeScript's type checking.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript discriminated union type to define component props with distinct variants
Implement a React component that accepts and renders content based on discriminated union props
Apply type narrowing techniques to safely access variant-specific properties within component logic
Configure event handlers that manipulate component state based on the active discriminated union variant
Initialize and update component state that controls which discriminated union variant is rendered
Integrate multiple UI elements that bind to different properties of the discriminated union variants
Render conditional UI structures that display content specific to each discriminated union variant

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing modules in TypeScript
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, enabling React and state management functionality.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using the correct import syntax.

steps.title: Define the discriminated union types
steps.instruction: Below the imports, define two TypeScript interface types named SuccessMessage and ErrorMessage. Both should have a common property called 'type' with literal string values ('success' and 'error' respectively), and different additional properties: SuccessMessage should have a 'message' property (string), and ErrorMessage should have a 'reason' property (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword to define each type. Remember that discriminated unions share a common discriminant property (here 'type') with literal values.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Define SuccessMessage and ErrorMessage interfaces here
steps.expectedOutcome: Two TypeScript interfaces are defined with a common discriminant property 'type' and different additional properties, forming a discriminated union.
successCriteria: SuccessMessage interface has type: 'success' and message: string; ErrorMessage interface has type: 'error' and reason: string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that both interfaces have the correct literal string values for 'type' and the proper additional properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The types aren't defined correctly. Ensure you have two interfaces with a common 'type' property (with literal values) and different additional properties.

steps.title: Create the union type for props
steps.instruction: Create a union type named MessageProps that combines the SuccessMessage and ErrorMessage interfaces using the pipe operator.
steps.hint: Use the TypeScript union type syntax: type MessageProps = SuccessMessage | ErrorMessage;
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: union type combining two interfaces
type VehicleProps = CarProps | BikeProps;
steps.expectedOutcome: A MessageProps union type is defined that can be either SuccessMessage or ErrorMessage.
successCriteria: MessageProps union type is created using the pipe operator to combine both interface types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the pipe operator (|) to combine both interface types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The union type wasn't created correctly. Remember to use 'type MessageProps = SuccessMessage | ErrorMessage;' syntax.

steps.title: Create the main component with typed props
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MessageDisplay that takes MessageProps as its props parameter and returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a component with typed props using the MessageProps union type you created earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: A MessageDisplay component is defined with properly typed props.
successCriteria: MessageDisplay is a functional component that accepts MessageProps as its props parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure MessageDisplay accepts MessageProps as its props parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named MessageDisplay that takes MessageProps as props.

steps.title: Initialize state with union type
steps.instruction: Inside your MessageDisplay component, initialize a useState hook with the MessageProps union type. Set the default value to a SuccessMessage variant with a message property.
steps.hint: Use useState<MessageProps> to type the state. Provide an initial object with type: 'success' and a message string.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: typed state initialization
const [data, setData] = useState<{ id: number; name: string }>({ id: 1, name: 'Example' });
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed state variable ready to hold either a success or error message variant.
successCriteria: A useState hook is declared with MessageProps type and initialized with a success variant object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to type useState with MessageProps and provide a default success object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using useState with the MessageProps type and providing a proper initial value.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering based on discriminant
steps.instruction: Inside the MessageDisplay component, use an if/else or switch statement on the 'type' property to return different JSX for each variant of the union.
steps.hint: Check the 'type' property of the props object. For 'success', return a paragraph with the message. For 'error', return a paragraph with the message and error code.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now conditionally render different JSX based on the 'type' property of the props.
successCriteria: The component uses an if/else or switch statement to check the 'type' property and returns appropriate JSX for each variant.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking the 'type' property and returning JSX for both 'success' and 'error' variants.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering isn't correctly implemented. Check that you're using the 'type' property to distinguish between the union variants and returning appropriate JSX for each.

steps.title: Render the success variant content
steps.instruction: Inside the conditional rendering for the success branch, render a paragraph element that displays the success message.
steps.hint: Use the props.message property within the success branch to access the message string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The success branch now displays the success message in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: The success branch contains a paragraph element that renders props.message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're rendering a paragraph element with the message property inside the success branch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The success branch should display the message in a paragraph element. Check that you're inside the correct conditional branch.

steps.title: Render the error variant content
steps.instruction: In the error branch of your conditional rendering, return JSX that displays the error-specific properties: the message and errorCode.
steps.hint: After the success branch's if statement, add an else if (props.type === 'error') block. Inside, return JSX that uses props.message and props.errorCode.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now handles both union branches: it renders content for success messages and will render content for error messages when the type is 'error'.
successCriteria: An else if (props.type === 'error') branch is added that returns JSX containing props.message and props.errorCode.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you check for props.type === 'error' and return JSX that uses both props.message and props.errorCode.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error branch is missing or incomplete. Add an else if (props.type === 'error') block that returns JSX displaying the message and errorCode.

steps.title: Add a button to switch to success state
steps.instruction: Inside the MessageDisplay component, add a button element with an onClick handler that sets the state to a SuccessMessage object. The button text should be 'Show Success'.
steps.hint: Use the useState setter function to update the state with an object matching the SuccessMessage interface.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button that updates state
<button onClick={() => setState({ type: 'success', message: 'Done!' })}>
  Show Success
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Show Success' appears in the component, which when clicked will update the state to a success message object.
successCriteria: The component contains a button element with onClick handler that sets state to a SuccessMessage object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure the onClick handler properly sets the state to a SuccessMessage object with the correct structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or its onClick handler is missing or incorrect. Review how to create a button and update state with a discriminated union value.

steps.title: Add a button to switch to error state
steps.instruction: Add a second button next to the existing one with an onClick handler that sets the state to an ErrorMessage object containing a message and errorCode.
steps.hint: Create a button element with onClick that calls setState with an object matching the ErrorMessage interface. Place it after the first button.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding another button with different state
<button onClick={() => setState({ type: 'error', message: 'Something went wrong', errorCode: 404 })}>
  Simulate Error
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two buttons: one switches to success state, the new one switches to error state.
successCriteria: A second button is added with onClick that sets state to an ErrorMessage object containing message and errorCode properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check that the onClick handler sets state to a complete ErrorMessage object with type, message, and errorCode.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button to switch to error state is missing or incorrect. Add a button with onClick that sets state to an object matching the ErrorMessage interface.

steps.title: Add the component to the app
steps.instruction: Create a main App component that renders the MessageDisplay component.
steps.hint: Define a functional component named App that returns the MessageDisplay component.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and renders the MessageDisplay component.
successCriteria: A functional component named App is created and returns the MessageDisplay component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a component named App that returns MessageDisplay.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not correctly defined. Create a functional component named App that renders MessageDisplay.

steps.title: Test the type-safe switching
steps.instruction: Click the 'Switch to Success' button to see the component render success content,
steps.hint: Observe how TypeScript correctly narrows the state type based on the 'type' property when you click each button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component should render green success text when in success state and red error text with error code when in error state. Clicking the buttons should switch between these states.
successCriteria: Both buttons are clicked and the component correctly renders different content based on the state's 'type' property
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made progress, but try clicking both buttons to fully test the type-safe switching. Observe how the component renders different content based on whether state.type is 'success' or 'error'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The type-safe switching isn't working as expected. Make sure you click both buttons and observe how TypeScript's type narrowing ensures you only access properties appropriate for each state variant.

steps.instruction: click the 'Switch to Error' button to see error content.
steps.hint: Observe how TypeScript correctly narrows the state type based on the 'type' property when you click each button.
